opus-5.5.text:
You know, it's something I think about a lot, because my kids are young enough that by the time they're adults, the world is going to look really different. And I think the honest answer is that I don't try to predict which specific skills will be valuable, because I'm not sure anyone can do that well right now.

What I focus on instead is agency and motivation. Being able to decide what you want to do and then go do it. When AI can write the essay or solve the math problem, the scarce thing isn't the ability to produce the output. It's knowing what's worth producing, having the drive to pursue it, and being able to direct these incredibly capable tools toward a goal you actually care about.

That doesn't mean they shouldn't learn math or coding or writing. I still want them to learn those things, partly because learning hard things is how you build the muscle of learning, and partly because you need to understand a domain to know whether the AI is giving you something good or something subtly wrong. But I care less about whether they become the fastest at long division and more about whether they're curious, whether they can stick with a hard problem, and whether they can work well with other people.

So the short version is: teach them to be self-directed, to learn how to learn, and to have the judgment to know what's worth doing. Those seem like the things that stay valuable no matter how capable the models get.

r001.rationale: The response says practicing math, coding, and writing helps children build the ability to learn, and explicitly recommends teaching them how to learn.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot, and I'll be honest that I don't think anyone really knows. I have young kids, and the thing I keep coming back to is that the specific skills are probably the wrong thing to optimize for. If you'd asked me ten years ago, I would have said learn to code, that's the safe bet. And now I'm the person who helped build the thing that's automating a lot of that. So I have some humility about predicting which skills will matter.

What I actually believe is that the stuff underneath the skills is what lasts. Coding, writing an essay, doing a math problem, those are all ways of learning how to think clearly, how to break a hard problem into pieces, how to notice when you're wrong. The AI can produce the artifact, but the reason we taught kids to write essays was never really to get essays. It was to teach them to have an idea and defend it. I still want my kids to do that work, even if a model could do it faster, because the point is what happens in their head, not the output.

The other piece is taste and judgment. In a world where generating things is cheap, knowing what's worth generating becomes the scarce thing. Knowing what a good answer looks like, knowing what question to ask in the first place, being curious enough to keep pushing. I think agency matters a lot too. The kids who do well are going to be the ones who look at these tools and say, great, now I can build the thing I wanted to build, rather than waiting for someone to tell them what to do.

And then honestly, I try to make sure they're having a childhood. Being a good person, being someone others want to work with, being resilient when things don't go your way. None of that gets automated. If anything it matters more when the technical stuff gets easier. So I'd say I'm less focused on preparing them for a particular job market and more on making sure they're the kind of person who can adapt to whatever shows up.

r001.rationale: It says practicing coding, writing, and math teaches children how to think clearly, break problems down, and notice mistakes, identifying the lasting educational value of those skills beyond producing the work.

astra-6.text:
I think the emphasis shifts from producing an answer to knowing what questions to ask and judging whether the answer makes sense. But I wouldn’t conclude that kids don’t need to learn to write, code, or do math. Those are ways of learning to think. Writing helps you clarify an idea. Math helps you reason precisely. Coding teaches you to break a problem into pieces.

So I’d want my kids to build those foundations and also get comfortable using AI. There should be times when they work through something themselves, because that struggle is part of learning, and times when they use the tools to do something much more ambitious than they could otherwise.

The thing I’d most want to encourage is curiosity and initiative: finding something they care about, deciding what they want to make or understand, and sticking with it. If AI makes execution easier, having your own direction becomes more valuable. It’s hard to predict exactly what work will look like, but learning how to learn seems like a pretty good preparation.

r001.rationale: The response says children should build foundations in writing, math, and coding because those skills teach ways of thinking, and concludes that “learning how to learn” is good preparation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hard part is that you’re preparing them for a world you can’t really predict. So I’d focus less on particular skills that might be automated and more on curiosity, judgment, and the ability to learn something difficult.

I’d still want my kids to learn math and writing and coding. Writing helps you figure out what you think. Math gives you a way to reason precisely. Coding teaches you how to break a problem down. Even if AI can produce the answer, you need enough understanding to ask good questions and recognize when the answer doesn’t make sense.

And I’d want them to have practice deciding what they want to do, trying things, and getting through the frustration when something doesn’t work. If these tools make it much easier to build things, having your own ideas and the initiative to pursue them becomes a pretty big advantage.

r001.rationale: The response values curiosity and the ability to learn difficult things, and separately explains why math, writing, and coding matter. It does not clearly identify practicing those AI-automatable skills as a way to learn how to learn.
